Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Vignette:
Koa, a 39-year-old airline pilot, presented with a deep weariness that seemed to settle in his eyes. The difficulties he now faced had begun some two years prior, following a terrifying encounter one late evening. He had been driving his young daughter home from a relative’s house when a police car, seemingly out of nowhere, pulled them over. The officer approached aggressively, shining a blinding flashlight directly into the car, his face mere inches from Koa’s window as he shouted questions. Koa remembered the overwhelming feeling of being trapped, the officer’s proximity a suffocating threat, and the chilling fear that gripped him, not just for himself, but for his child silently crying in the back seat. A wave of nausea had washed over him then, a visceral response to the helplessness and terror. Though they were eventually allowed to leave with a warning, the memory of that night became an indelible scar.

Now, remembering the event brought back the same terror he had felt at the time, a raw, physiological reliving of that fear. His memories of that night felt more real and vivid than any ordinary recollection, as if they had happened moments ago, yet the extremity of the experience made it hard for him to truly believe it had happened to him at all. It was a paradox he lived with daily.

These memories and the fear they evoked had begun to reshape Koa’s world. The physical proximity of others, particularly strangers, now triggered an intense unease. In the cramped cockpit, or navigating bustling airport terminals, he found himself constantly on edge, hyper-aware of every person near him. He had taken to arriving earlier for flights, trying to avoid the peak crowds, and often ate alone in quieter areas of the crew lounge. Driving with other people, even colleagues or friends, had become a source of profound anxiety. He found himself making excuses to drive alone, preferring the isolation, even if it meant longer commutes. And the most unsettling trigger was the feeling of nausea itself; any slight stomach upset would immediately transport him back to the terror of that night, his heart pounding, convinced something terrible was about to unfold.

His professional life, once a source of pride and stability, was now a constant battleground. As an airline pilot, delays were an inherent part of the job, but for Koa, they had transformed into harbingers of doom. When something took longer than expected – a gate delay, an air traffic control hold, a prolonged mechanical check – he would assume something bad was happening, his mind racing through catastrophic scenarios. He’d jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people: the sudden clang of a meal cart, the unexpected chime of a passenger call button, or even the loud cough of a co-pilot. Every unexpected noise felt like an alarm. Compounding this, he now felt profoundly threatened by strangers approaching him, even in ordinary situations. Interacting with ground crew, flight attendants, and especially passengers, had become an exhausting ordeal, requiring immense effort to maintain a calm exterior. He had become withdrawn, rarely engaging in casual conversation, his vigilance consuming his energy.

Over the past year, the accumulated stress had taken its toll. His marriage had crumbled, his wife unable to understand his increasing irritability and withdrawal, his constant need for solitude. He had started to take more sick days, citing vague illnesses, to avoid the overwhelming sensory input of the airport and the constant fear of delays. His performance reviews, once stellar, had begun to show subtle signs of distraction and an unusual rigidity in his decision-making. He was terrified of losing the career he had dedicated his life to, yet every flight felt like an unbearable challenge. The fear of making a mistake, of missing a critical detail because his mind was consumed by threat, loomed large. What finally brought him to seek help was a near-panic attack during a routine pre-flight check when a minor technical delay sent his anxiety spiraling, convincing him that the aircraft was catastrophically compromised. He knew then he could no longer manage this alone, fearing that his internal turmoil would one day jeopardize the lives of his passengers.
